title: An unramified map of integral curves has nonsingleton image
statement: Let $k$ be a field and $X,Y$ be curves over $k$, meaning separated integral finite-type $k$-schemes of dimension one [def-pc-curve]. Let $h:X\to Y$ be a $k$-morphism. If $h$ is unramified [def-weil-unramified-morphism], then its image contains at least two points. More generally, for every nonempty open subscheme $V\subseteq X$, if $h|_V:V\to Y$ is unramified, then $V$ is again a curve over $k$ and the image of $h|_V$ contains at least two points. No smoothness, normality, perfection of $k$, or rational point is assumed.

proof.text: Let $V\subseteq X$ be nonempty open. It is integral: each nonempty affine open of $V$ is a nonempty affine open of $X$ and thus has a domain as its ring of functions, exactly [def-pc-integral-scheme]. It is separated over $k$ as well. Indeed [lem-weil-pbc-open-fibre-product] identifies $V\times_kV$ with the open subset of $X\times_kX$ where both projections lie in $V$. The diagonal of $V$ is the restriction of the closed diagonal of $X$ to that open: its inverse image in $X$ is $V$, and its structure-sheaf map is the restricted quotient map. A closed subset remains closed in an open subspace and a surjective sheaf map remains surjective on restriction. Thus this restricted diagonal is a closed immersion, giving separatedness by [def-weil-proper-morphism].

source.place: Tag 01OK, definition-integral; separatedness by restriction of the diagonal, schemes.tex Tag 01KK, definition-separated; open fibre product Tag 01JR

proof.text: The scheme $\operatorname{Spec}k$ is Noetherian: its only point has local ring $k$, whose only ideals are $(0)$ and $(1)$, and its one-point space is quasi-compact. Since $X$ is finite type over it, [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-over-noetherian] makes $X$ Noetherian. Apply [lem-sfb-noetherian-open-immersion-qc] to $j:V\hookrightarrow X$; its target is locally Noetherian, so $j$ is quasi-compact. Then [lem-weil-pbc-qc-open-immersion-finite-type] makes $j$ finite type, and clause (1) of [lem-sfb-finite-type-composition-base-change], applied to $j$ and $X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$, makes $V$ finite type over $k$. This checks the global finite-type condition even for a non-affine open $V$.

source.place: Tags 01T6, lemma-finite-type-noetherian; 01T3, lemma-composition-finite-type; properties.tex Tag 01OX, lemma-immersion-into-noetherian; finite type criterion Tags 01T0 and 01T2

proof.text: The dimension in [def-pc-curve] is the supremum of local-ring dimensions. By [lem-pc-scheme-dimension-local-rings], it equals topological Krull dimension, for both $X$ and $V$. The hypotheses of [lem-sc-integral-locally-algebraic-opens-dimension] hold for $X$: it is integral and its structure map is locally of finite type, since it is finite type. Hence the nonempty open $V$ has the same topological dimension as $X$, namely one. Together with Steps 1 and 2, this says precisely that $V$ is a curve over $k$ in [def-pc-curve].

Apply the following argument with $(T,g)=(X,h)$, or with $(T,g)=(V,h|_V)$ under the respective unramified hypothesis. In either case $T$ is an integral curve, so it is nonempty and irreducible by [def-pc-integral-scheme], and its topological dimension is one by [lem-pc-scheme-dimension-local-rings]. If its image has fewer than two points, nonemptiness gives an image point $y$ and $g^{-1}(y)=T$. Unramifiedness includes local finite type by [def-weil-unramified-morphism]. For each $t\in T$ the whole $T$ is an unramified neighbourhood, so the final, subspace formulation of [lem-weil-pbc-unramified-fibre-point-isolated] says that $\{t\}$ is open in $g^{-1}(y)=T$. Hence $T$ is discrete. If it had distinct points $t,u$, its nonempty opens $\{t\}$ and $\{u\}$ would be disjoint, contradicting irreducibility. Thus $T$ has exactly one point. The only nonempty irreducible closed subset of a one-point space is the whole space; the chain definition [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension] therefore gives dimension zero, contradicting dimension one. Thus each asserted image contains at least two points, whether $y$ would have been closed or generic.
